acceptance_criteria: All SQL behind trait. CI uses PostgreSQL. SQLite works locally. Oracle stub compiles. Migration dirs documented.
description:
## Why this issue exists

stoa-mail currently uses `sqlx::AnyPool` and has two migration directories (SQLite and PostgreSQL dialect), but all SQL is written inline throughout business logic files. The `sqlx::query!` macros compile-time-check against a single `DATABASE_URL`, making it impossible to have a single verified build for more than one backend simultaneously.

Regulated and enterprise customers need to run stoa-mail against their existing managed database infrastructure: AWS RDS (PostgreSQL or Oracle), Azure Database for PostgreSQL, on-premise Oracle, or operator-managed PostgreSQL. SQLite is appropriate for local development and testing only.

Oracle is not supported by sqlx at all, requiring a separate driver (`oracle` crate / OCI, or ODBC). Without a trait boundary, Oracle support would require forking business logic.

## What needs to be done

### Phase 1 — MailStore trait

Define a `MailStore` trait in `stoa-mail` (or `stoa-core`) that exposes all database operations as async methods. Move all inline `sqlx::query` calls out of business logic and into a `SqlxMailStore` struct that implements the trait.

The trait should group operations by domain:
- `UserStore`: resolve_user_id, create_user, set_password_hash, get_password_hash
- `TokenStore`: issue_token, validate_token, revoke_token, purge_expired
- `MailboxStore`: list_mailboxes, get_mailbox, create_mailbox, delete_mailbox
- `MessageStore`: insert_message, get_message, list_messages, set_flags
- `StateStore`: get_state_version, bump_state_version, append_change_log
- `SubscriptionStore`: get_subscriptions, set_subscription

A single `MailStore` supertrait combines all of these. Business logic receives `&dyn MailStore` (or `Arc<dyn MailStore>`).

### Phase 2 — PostgreSQL as canonical backend

- Promote `migrations_pg/` as the primary migration directory.
- Switch all `sqlx::query!` macros to compile-time-check against PostgreSQL (`DATABASE_URL` in CI points to a real PG instance or `sqlx offline` data captured against PG).
- SQLite remains supported via `sqlx::AnyPool` for local dev/test, but is no longer the compile-time-checked target. Accept that SQLite may have minor dialect drift on edge cases.
- Document: SQLite = dev/test, PostgreSQL = production/staging.

### Phase 3 — Migration portability

Audit all migrations for dialect-specific constructs. Where PostgreSQL and SQLite diverge, document the canonical PG form and the SQLite approximation. Consolidate the two migration dirs into one PG-canonical set plus a SQLite compatibility shim if needed.

Add a third migration set skeleton for MySQL/MariaDB (covers RDS MySQL, Azure Database for MySQL) — low effort once PG is canonical since sqlx supports MySQL natively via `AnyPool`.

### Phase 4 — Oracle adapter (stub)

Define an `OracleMailStore` struct that implements `MailStore` using the `oracle` crate (OCI bindings). In Phase 4 this can be a stub (all methods return `Err(not_implemented)`) — the point is to prove the trait boundary is sufficient and to document what an Oracle implementer would need.

Full Oracle implementation is deferred until a concrete customer requirement exists.

## Acceptance criteria

- All SQL is behind the `MailStore` trait; no `sqlx::query` calls in business logic files
- `SqlxMailStore` implements the trait; passes all existing tests against both SQLite and PostgreSQL
- CI runs against PostgreSQL (not SQLite) as the canonical backend; `sqlx offline` data committed for PostgreSQL
- SQLite still works for `cargo test` locally without a running PG instance
- `OracleMailStore` stub exists and compiles; its existence documents the Oracle integration surface
- Migration dirs consolidated; differences between SQLite and PG dialects are documented inline

## Design notes

- Use `Arc<dyn MailStore + Send + Sync>` in the `AppState` struct — this is the idiomatic axum pattern.
- `async-trait` crate required until async-fn-in-trait stabilises (AFIT landed in Rust 1.75 but has limitations with `dyn`; check status at implementation time).
- RDS for PostgreSQL = PostgreSQL, no additional work.
- RDS for Oracle = Oracle; covered by Phase 4.
- MySQL/RDS MySQL: sqlx native support, Phase 3 migration work covers it.
- Do NOT use an ORM (SeaORM, Diesel) — sqlx with a hand-written trait is simpler, more portable, and avoids macro-heavy compilation overhead.
design: The MailStore trait is the correct seam for Oracle. sqlx cannot be extended to support Oracle; a separate impl is the only path. The trait also enables in-memory mock stores for unit tests, which currently require a real SQLite file even for logic tests that don't care about persistence.
title: Database backend abstraction: MailStore trait + multi-backend support
